tools/actual-budget.heading: Start with a budget, not a server.

qas.a: Not for local budgeting in the desktop app. Device sync, bank sync and the API need a server. Mobile use is through a browser or installed web app, not a native phone app.
Actual is local-first. A sync server keeps a copy for your devices. Bank connections are optional external services; manual entries and file imports are an alternative.
A self-hosted server needs updates, HTTPS for other devices and backups. A hosted option can reduce server work, but you still need a way to export and restore your budget.

tools/almalinux.heading: Choose your release line, then plan in years, not months.

qas.a: AlmaLinux publishes two stable lines (10.x and 9.x), both compatible with RHEL and maintained for years. New installs usually take the newest line; match 9.x when the software or documentation you follow requires it.

qas.q: Will it run on my hardware?
qas.a: Standard servers, PCs and virtual machines on x86-64 or ARM64. If the machine is more than about a decade old, check the release notes' CPU baseline before downloading.

qas.q: What happens to what is on the disk?
qas.a: The installer can erase the disk, use free space, or share it with another system. It preserves nothing you do not partition around, so back up first.

tools/blackarch.heading: Decide: a full system, or a tool layer on Arch.

qas.a: Two routes: the full BlackArch system image, or adding its repository to an existing Arch install and pulling only the tools you need. The layer keeps your current system; the full install replaces it.
It is a penetration-testing toolkit, not a general desktop. Its 2,800+ tools assume you know why you need them, and they are only for systems you own or have explicit permission to test.

qas.q: How much disk does it need?
qas.a: The complete tool collection needs substantial space. Installing by category, or the slim image, keeps it lean.

tools/debian.heading: Try it live, then let stable be boring.

qas.a: The live images (GNOME, KDE or Xfce) run from a USB stick without touching the disk - the easiest hardware check. The installer images go straight to installing.
Stable is the default for a reason: reliability over novelty, with years of security updates. Testing and unstable exist for people who accept breakage.

Standard 64-bit PCs are the target, but Wi-Fi cards and very new graphics hardware are the usual exceptions. Official images can include non-free firmware for hardware that needs it; the live image is the cheapest way to check your machine.

tools/fedora.heading: Workstation first; the other editions are different downloads.

qas.a: Workstation is the GNOME desktop and the right first trial. Server, KDE Plasma, IoT and CoreOS are separate images for separate goals, not options inside one installer.
A new release about every six months, each supported for roughly thirteen. Upgrading between releases is a normal, supported path.
The live image boots from USB for a no-risk look; the installer can reclaim a disk or share it. Back up whatever you keep before partitioning.

tools/freebsd.heading: A complete Unix system, not a Linux distribution.

qas.q: Is FreeBSD right for my goal?
qas.a: It suits servers, storage and network appliances, and people who want an integrated base system. Desktop use is possible but more hands-on than a Linux desktop.
Standard 64-bit PCs and virtual machines; other architectures have their own support tiers. A VM or spare machine is the sensible first install.
Prebuilt packages cover most needs; the ports collection builds from source when you need compile-time options changed. Both are normal, documented routes.

tools/kali-linux.heading: A workbench for authorized security testing, not a daily desktop.

qas.q: Should this be my main OS?
qas.a: OffSec itself recommends against Kali as a general-purpose desktop for people unfamiliar with Linux. A VM or live image keeps your main system untouched.
Pre-built virtual machines are the fastest safe start; live images run from USB with optional persistence; the installer is for dedicated machines.
Only systems you own or have explicit permission to test. The tools are dual-use, and this listing assumes lawful, authorized work.

tools/linux-mint.heading: A familiar desktop first; codecs and drivers stay your choice.

qas.a: Cinnamon is Mint's flagship and the familiar-layout choice; MATE and Xfce are lighter alternatives. All three are free downloads from the same page.
The start-style menu, taskbar and tray are deliberately traditional. Update and driver tools are Mint's own, and proprietary drivers are an opt-in, not a default.
Multimedia codecs are an install-time checkbox, not bundled by default - tick the box if you want them.

tools/nixos.heading: Your whole system becomes one editable file.

qas.a: Packages, services, users and settings live in /etc/nixos/configuration.nix. Rebuilding applies changes atomically, and every generation stays in the boot menu.

qas.q: What if an upgrade breaks something?
qas.a: Pick the previous generation at boot and you are back. Rollback is the core design, not a recovery hack.
Yes: daily use means editing Nix expressions. The graphical installer gets you a desktop, but comfort with configuration files is the price of admission.

tools/omarchy.heading: One opinionated desktop, installed as a finished system.

qas.a: An Arch base with a curated Hyprland desktop, fixed defaults and themed tools - one person's choices applied as a complete system, not assembled piece by piece.

qas.q: Can I keep my current setup?
qas.a: No: it installs as its own OS (x86, ARM64 and Apple Silicon images). Treat it as a dedicated system, not a layer over what you have.

qas.q: What if I want to change things?
qas.a: It is Arch underneath, so anything is changeable - but the point is the curated defaults. Heavy customization fights the project's grain.

tools/opensuse.heading: Rolling or regular release - pick the identity first.

qas.a: Tumbleweed is the rolling release: always current, tested before publishing. Leap follows regular releases aligned with SUSE's enterprise line. They are different systems, not versions of each other.

qas.q: What if a rolling update goes wrong?
qas.a: The default Btrfs layout takes automatic snapshots; boot the previous snapshot and roll back.
Standard 64-bit PCs and VMs, with live images to check hardware before you commit.

tools/opnsense.heading: A dedicated router, not an app on your desktop.

qas.a: A spare x86 machine with two network ports, an appliance, or a virtual machine. It becomes your network's gateway; it is not software you add to a PC you keep using.
This listing covers the free Community edition. The Business Edition is Deciso's commercial line with its own terms.
The installer erases the target device. Test in a VM first, and keep the existing router until the replacement passes traffic.

tools/parrot.heading: Home edition for daily use, Security for the lab.

qas.a: Home is a privacy-minded daily desktop with no attack tooling. Security is the penetration-testing and forensics platform. HTB, IoT and cloud editions serve narrower uses.
The Home edition, yes. The Security edition assumes lab use: tools you run only against systems you own or may test.
A standard 64-bit PC, run live from USB, in a VM, or installed. Security tooling appreciates RAM; the desktop itself is Debian-modest.
The NVIDIA image bundles the driver for newer GeForce cards; the standard image covers everything else. Picking right at download saves a driver detour.
System76's own desktop environment with optional auto-tiling - not GNOME, despite the Ubuntu base. It is the default, not an add-on.
Standard 64-bit PCs, and naturally System76's own machines. A live session from the USB stick checks compatibility before you install.

tools/qubes.heading: Security by isolation - check the hardware before anything else.

qas.q: Will it run on my machine?
qas.a: Qubes has unusually strict requirements: hardware virtualization (VT-x/VT-d or AMD-V/IOMMU) enabled in firmware, generous RAM, and a compatible network card. Read the system requirements first.
Work happens in separate virtual machines called qubes: one for banking, one for random browsing, disposable ones for risky files. It is a deliberate workflow change, not a themed Linux.
A live USB session gives a basic look, but real evaluation needs an install. Use Qubes' own backup tool before migrating anything into it.

tools/tails.heading: You do not install it - you carry it.

qas.a: Tails runs from a USB stick and leaves no trace on the computer by default. There is no installer in the usual sense: the stick is the system.
Nowhere, unless you set up the encrypted persistent storage on the stick. Everything else vanishes on shutdown, by design.
Tor protects connections, not identity mistakes: logging into personal accounts can still identify you, and closed-source firmware is included so more hardware works.

tools/ubuntu.heading: Pick the track first: LTS for stability, interim for currency.

qas.a: LTS releases arrive every two years with five years of free security updates, extendable with Ubuntu Pro (free for personal use on up to five machines). Interim releases suit people who enjoy upgrading often.
A live desktop to try first, then a guided install. The optional third-party software box adds proprietary graphics drivers and extra media formats - your choice, ticked or not.
LTS-to-LTS upgrades are a supported path. Back up first, as with any OS upgrade.
CalyxOS supports specific Google Pixel models plus a small set of others on its device list. The official install page is the only authority - check it before anything else.
The installer unlocks the bootloader and flashes the system; unlocking wipes the device. Whether relocking is safe depends on the device, so follow the official guide exactly.
microG provides compatibility for apps that expect Google services. It is a compatibility choice, not full Google Play; banking and integrity-checked apps vary.

tools/grapheneos.heading: Only Pixels, and only supported ones.

qas.a: GrapheneOS supports current Google Pixel models only, chosen for their hardware security and update support. Check the official device list first; an old or unsupported Pixel is a no.
The official web installer unlocks the bootloader, flashes GrapheneOS, and locks the bootloader again. Unlocking and locking wipe the phone - everything on it is gone.
Returning to stock Android means flashing Google's factory images through a similar process. Possible, but plan the install, not the rescue.

tools/lineageos.heading: New life for older phones, model by model.

qas.a: LineageOS builds are per-device: the wiki's device list says exactly which models, which build, and which instructions. A similar model does not count.
An unlock, a custom recovery, then the LineageOS image - and the unlock wipes the phone. Relocking can make a device unusable, so leave the bootloader as the official instructions say.
Not included. A separate add-on package provides them if you want it; the wrong package or version causes boot problems, so follow the device wiki page.
You install Ventoy onto a USB stick once, then copy ISO files onto it like regular files. Boot the stick and pick from a menu of everything it holds - no re-imaging between systems.
The target USB stick, completely, during setup. The computers you later boot are untouched until you choose something inside a booted installer.
Most PCs with UEFI or legacy BIOS; Secure Boot needs the enrollment step the documentation describes. ISOs can be copied on from Linux, Windows or macOS.

tools/ublock-origin.heading: Check your browser's extension rules first.

qas.a: Firefox is the project's own recommendation. Chrome's store no longer carries full uBlock Origin - the separate uBlock Origin Lite is the official Manifest V3 option there.

qas.q: Is the store listing the real one?
qas.a: Install only through the links in the project's README, and check the developer identity and store entry ID. Lookalike extensions trade on the name.
It filters what pages load: ads, trackers, malware domains. It is not an antivirus, and an over-aggressive list can break sites - the per-site power button is the first fix.

tools/audacity.heading: Install once, edit locally; nothing leaves the machine.

qas.a: The project's download page names the supported package for each distribution; Windows and macOS have the project's own installers.
In files you choose: .aup3 project files and whatever you export. Editing never uploads anything.
No. Recording, editing and exporting are fully offline.

tools/beancount.heading: Your ledger is a text file you own.

qas.a: Beancount is the engine: a Python package with the bean-check command. Add Fava when you want a web view over the same files.
In plain-text ledger files. They work with Git, any editor, and whatever backup tool you already trust.
Nobody but you: it runs locally with no account or service. Fava reads the same local files.

tools/blender.heading: One big download; no account, no cloud.

qas.a: The project's own builds from blender.org can sit side by side, so you can keep several versions. Distribution packages work too but may lag.
In .blend files wherever you save them. Renders and caches go where you point them.
Any reasonably modern 64-bit machine; heavier scenes want a supported GPU. Check the requirements page before a big project.

tools/cryptomator.heading: Encrypt first, then let any cloud sync it.

qas.a: It encrypts files into a vault before they sync. It works alongside Nextcloud, Syncthing or any cloud folder - it is not a sync service itself.
The vault is an ordinary folder of encrypted files. Your password unlocks it; lose the password and the files are unrecoverable.
This listing covers the desktop app. The mobile apps are separate products with their own terms.

tools/cura.heading: Slicing is local; the cloud extras are optional.

qas.a: The AppImage on Linux, or the project's installers for Windows and macOS. UltiMaker's cloud account features are optional, not required for slicing.
Profiles exist for many printer brands, not just UltiMaker. Check your model in the printer list before committing.
Both are listed and both are free; trying the same model in each is normal.
The install page's AppImage covers x86-64 and aarch64; the Flatpak exists but lacks the AI features, per the project's own note.
Into sidecar files next to your photos; the originals are never altered. Back up the sidecars with the photos.
darktable develops RAW photos; Immich stores and browses the library. They pair well and answer different questions.

tools/dbeaver.heading: A client for databases you already have.

qas.a: DBeaver Community is the free Apache-2.0 edition from dbeaver.io. PRO features are separate commercial products; this listing covers Community.
No server of its own: it connects to databases you point it at. A sample SQLite file is enough to explore.
In the workspace on your machine. Saved database credentials stay local - treat them like passwords.

tools/digikam.heading: A librarian for big photo collections, on your disk.

qas.a: The download page's AppImage (needs glibc 2.31 or newer) is the direct route on Linux; installers cover Windows and macOS.
Your photos stay where they are; digiKam catalogs them in its own database files. Tags can be written into file metadata if you choose.
digiKam organizes; darktable develops RAW files. Many people point both at the same folders.

tools/drawio-desktop.heading: Diagrams as files, offline by default.

qas.a: The installer for your system on the releases page; Homebrew's cask is Homebrew's packaging, not the project's.
As .drawio files (or embedded in PNG/SVG) wherever you put them - easy to keep in Git or sync yourself.
This is the GPL-3.0 desktop build. The draw.io web editor is a separate repository under Apache-2.0.

tools/flameshot.heading: Screenshots with markup, straight from the keyboard.

qas.a: One command per distribution on the install page - run only the one for yours. Windows and macOS have their own packages.
Screenshot permissions differ by compositor; check the project's notes if captures come out blank.
To files or the clipboard. Nothing is uploaded unless you ask.

tools/gimp.heading: The veteran image editor, free as in freedom.

qas.a: AppImage, Flatpak or Snap on Linux (the Flathub listing is publisher-verified); installers for Windows and macOS.
GIMP covers retouching, compositing and painting. Krita leans toward painting, darktable toward RAW photos - pick per job.
Work saves as .xcf to keep layers; export to PNG or JPEG for sharing. Install plug-ins only from sources you trust.

tools/gnucash.heading: Ledger accounting in a file on your computer.

qas.q: Is it the same as Actual Budget?
qas.a: No: GnuCash is double-entry accounting; Actual is envelope budgeting. Pick by how you think about money.
In one file (or a database you configure). That file is the whole history - back it up.

qas.q: Can I import my bank's exports?
qas.a: It imports QIF and OFX files from banks and other tools. Test a small import before moving years of history.

tools/handbrake.heading: Convert video locally; nothing gets uploaded.

qas.a: Official builds skip the fdk-aac library because its license is GPL-incompatible, per the project's LICENSE notes.
Installers for Windows and macOS from the project; on Linux the distribution package or the Flatpak the documentation names.
Pick a built-in preset for your target device and run a short test clip before tweaking settings.

tools/hledger.heading: Accounting in plain text, three interfaces deep.

qas.a: A single binary: the command line, hledger-ui in the terminal, and hledger-web in a browser. It reads Ledger-format journals too.
In a plain-text journal file - Git-friendly, editor-friendly, future-proof.
Ledger is the C++ original; Beancount is the Python take with Fava's web view. All three are listed, and the formats differ.

tools/joplin.heading: Notes with sync you choose, end to end.

qas.a: The apps, under AGPL-3.0. Joplin Server carries a Personal Use License that is not open source, so it is not part of this listing.
Locally first; sync goes to a service you pick (Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, Joplin Cloud). End-to-end encryption is a setting worth turning on.
Set sync up on one device and let it finish before adding the next; the same account covers the mobile apps.

tools/kdenlive.heading: Multi-track video editing without a subscription.

qas.a: Distribution packages, the project's AppImage, or the Windows and macOS builds. The GitHub repository is a mirror of KDE's own.
Projects are files on your disk and source footage stays where you keep it. Rendering happens locally.

qas.q: Will it run on my machine?
qas.a: Timeline playback likes a decent CPU and GPU; proxy clips let slower machines edit big footage.

tools/keepassxc.heading: A password vault that is just a file.

qas.a: In one encrypted database file - no account, no server. You can sync that file with whatever you trust (Syncthing, Nextcloud, a USB stick); resolve sync conflicts when two devices edit at once, and keep backups.
The database file and its credentials: a master password, optionally combined with a key file or a hardware key. There is no recovery email; back the file up.
KeePassXC is the local-file route; Vaultwarden is the self-hosted vault with sharing. Both are listed.

tools/kopia.heading: Encrypted, deduplicated backups with a GUI or a CLI.

qas.a: Incremental snapshots to local disks, network storage or cloud storage. The same repository works from the command line or the desktop app.

qas.q: What should I do on day one?
qas.a: A trial restore of one folder. A backup you have never restored from is a hope, not a backup.
restic is the command-line-first alternative; Kopia adds the desktop app.

tools/krita.heading: Built by and for people who paint.

qas.a: Krita is for digital painting and illustration; GIMP for retouching and compositing. Both are free - try both.
Distribution packages, the AppImage, or the Windows and macOS builds. The GitHub repository is a mirror of KDE's infrastructure.
Native .kra files keep layers; export for sharing. It opens PSD files with caveats on exotic features.
It is the 2003 command-line original that inspired hledger and Beancount. Pick it if you want the classic.
In a text file of transactions; reports come from running ledger against it. Nothing leaves your machine.
Distribution packages on Linux, Homebrew on macOS.

tools/libreoffice.heading: The office suite that needs no account.

qas.a: Distribution packages on Linux; direct installers for Windows and macOS from libreoffice.org.
MPL-2.0 per the project's own licenses page. GitHub's mirror label says GPL-3.0, which does not match; the project's statement wins.
It reads and writes Microsoft formats with occasional layout drift on complex documents; its native format is ODF.

tools/logseq.heading: Local-first notes, with a beta worth treating as beta.

qas.a: The file-based version is the established one. The newer Database version is beta with a data-loss warning from the project itself - automated backups are your job either way.
As local Markdown or Org files linked into a graph, readable by any editor.
Real-time collaboration and its mobile sync are alpha. Local files plus your own sync (Syncthing, Git) is the stable route.

tools/mixxx.heading: Free DJ software that drives real hardware.

qas.a: DJ sets from your music library: controllers, effects, beat matching and recording.
Check the controller compatibility list before buying hardware; many popular controllers work out of the box.
On your machine. Music files stay wherever they are; Mixxx keeps its own library database.

tools/obs-studio.heading: Record or stream, straight from your desktop.

qas.a: Officially distributed as a Flatpak on Flathub and a PPA for Ubuntu 26.04 and newer; Windows and macOS builds come from the project.

qas.q: What should I do before the real recording?
qas.a: A short test: check audio sources, encoder settings and where the files land.
Recording to file needs nothing but disk space. Streaming needs a stream key from whatever platform you stream to.

qas.q: When is OpenSCAD the right tool?
qas.a: When you want exact, parametric models - mechanical parts and 3D printing - rather than sculpting. For sculpting, see Blender.
Distribution packages on Linux; downloads for Windows and macOS from the project.
Models are .scad text files - version them in Git like code. Export STL or 3MF for the slicer.

tools/pinta.heading: Simple image editing without the cockpit.

qas.a: For quick edits and drawing: layers, selections, effects, done. GIMP is there when you outgrow it.
Distribution packages or Flatpak on Linux; installers for Windows and macOS.
Original Pinta code is MIT, and it includes Paint.NET 3.36 code under that project's MIT terms.

tools/prusaslicer.heading: From model to print instructions, Prusa or not.

qas.a: Profiles cover Prusa printers and many other makes, with multi-material and resin support. Cura is the other big free slicer; both are listed.
Distribution packages or the project's own builds; an AppImage covers Linux.

qas.q: How do I trust a profile?
qas.a: Slice a known-good test model first before trusting a long print.
A single binary for cron jobs and scripts: encrypted, deduplicated snapshots to local or remote backends. Choose Kopia if you want a graphical app.

qas.q: What should I do on day one?
qas.a: Run restic restore on one snapshot early. Backups that were never restored are hopes, not backups.
The repository password - the only key to your data. Store it somewhere separate from the machine being backed up.

tools/signal-desktop.heading: The desktop app is a companion to your phone.

qas.q: Do I need the phone app?
qas.a: Yes: Signal Desktop links to the Signal account on your phone. It is not a standalone account, so set up the phone app first.
The client code. The messaging service it connects to is run by Signal - using the app means using their service.
On your devices. They sync from the phone at link time, and disappearing messages still disappear.

tools/simplex-chat.heading: Messaging with no user identifiers at all.

qas.a: They do not, by default: contacts connect through one-time links or QR codes. No user IDs exist to look up.

qas.q: Should I trust it for sensitive talk?
qas.a: Read the linked Trail of Bits security assessment and the project's documentation first, then decide.
The code is AGPL-3.0 and the protocols are described as open and public domain; the SimpleX names and logos are not covered by that license.

tools/standard-notes.heading: Encrypted notes, with a clear line between free and paid.

qas.a: The app and server code are public (AGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0), but not every feature is free: the plans page lists paid tiers, and self-hosted premium features need a subscription or offline plan.
Only if you will maintain it - the project documents the route, and it is real work. Decide before your notes pile up.

qas.q: What if I lose my password?
qas.a: Notes are encrypted end to end with it. Lose it and the notes are gone.

tools/super-productivity.heading: Tasks, time tracking and planning - offline first.

qas.a: No: the README says it collects no data and you decide where data lives. Local files are the default.
Optionally, through Dropbox, WebDAV or the project's SuperSync service. It can also import tasks from tools like GitHub and Jira.
Desktop apps for Linux, Windows and macOS, plus a web app; the quick start covers each route.

tools/taskwarrior.heading: To-do lists at the speed of the terminal.

qas.a: If you prefer the keyboard: tags, priorities, due dates and filters. For a web interface with sharing, see Vikunja.
Your distribution packages it (task or taskwarrior3 depending on the distro); Homebrew on macOS.
In local files - easy to back up or sync yourself. A separate sync server exists but is optional.

tools/thunderbird.heading: Your email, calendar and RSS in one free client.

qas.a: No: Thunderbird is a client that connects to accounts you already have. It is not mail hosting or a mail server.
Mail stores locally (and on your server per account settings). Everything lives in the profile folder - back it up.
The desktop code is MPL-2.0. The Thunderbird name and logo are Mozilla Foundation trademarks.
Distribution packages, or VideoLAN's own downloads. The GitHub repository is a mirror of VideoLAN's own.
VideoLAN, a non-profit; the code is GPL-2.0 or LGPL per its legal page.
No: files, discs and network streams on your own computer - no cloud involved.

tools/zotero.heading: A research library that lives on your machine.

qas.a: The AGPL-3.0 desktop client. The optional sync and storage service is run by the project and is a separate matter.
Locally: PDFs, notes and metadata on your disk. Sync is optional and tied to a free zotero.org account with storage limits.

qas.q: What should I install after the app?
qas.a: The browser connector for capturing sources, and the word-processor plugin for citations.

tools/adguard-home.heading: DNS filtering for the whole network, one small service.

qas.a: A single machine on your network that stays on: a Raspberry Pi, a small server or a Docker host. Devices point at it for DNS.
Filter rules, blocklists and query logs live on your AdGuard Home machine, not with AdGuard's company. The listing is the self-hosted server, separate from AdGuard's paid apps and hosted AdGuard DNS.
Updates, blocklist choices and the DHCP/DNS settings on your router. DNS filtering blocks domain lookups; it cannot remove every ad inside an allowed website or app.

tools/audiobookshelf.heading: Your audiobooks, your hardware, every device in sync.

qas.a: A server you run - Docker, the Debian/Ubuntu package or a NixOS module - plus the web player and the project's own Android and iOS apps.
Libraries, listening progress and stats stay on your hardware. Nothing routes through a third-party service.
Updates and storage for the audio files, and a backup of the library metadata if losing progress would hurt. It covers audio; Jellyfin is the usual video partner.

tools/beszel.heading: Lightweight monitoring: one hub, small agents.

qas.a: A web hub (Docker or a binary) plus a small agent on each system you want to watch. The hub alone collects no host metrics.
CPU, memory, disk, network and container stats with history live on your hub. Nothing leaves your machines for a hosted service.
The hub and one agent per machine, kept updated together. It gives charts and alerts without replacing a full metrics stack such as VictoriaMetrics plus Grafana.

tools/caddy.heading: A web server whose HTTPS just works.

qas.a: Any Linux server, a Docker container or a package repo install. Its headline feature is automatic HTTPS: it obtains and renews Let's Encrypt certificates without configuration.
Your sites and the Caddyfile live on your server. Certificates come from Let's Encrypt; no account with a vendor is required.
A short Caddyfile, updates, and the usual web-server care. It serves static files, reverse-proxies to apps and handles TLS renewal for you.

tools/copyparty.heading: A file server in a single Python file.

qas.a: Almost anywhere Python runs - one file, no database, no build step. Also available as Docker images and packages.
Whatever folder you point it at stays yours. Uploads, downloads, thumbnails and search run from that one process on your machine.
Almost nothing to start; more if you expose it. WebDAV, FTP, SFTP and SMB come from the same process, so plan access rules before opening ports.

tools/cryptpad.heading: A collaborative office suite the host cannot read.

qas.a: A Node.js server you host, or the project's own flagship instance. Documents, spreadsheets, slides, forms and boards are encrypted in the browser.
The server stores only encrypted content - the host cannot read your documents. Keys live in the links you share.
A real production service: updates, storage, and backup of the encrypted blobs. Developed by XWiki SAS; the hosted cryptpad.fr is run by the same team.

tools/fava.heading: A browser window onto your Beancount ledger.

qas.a: Runs locally against your own Beancount text files - it is not a hosted service. Beancount itself is listed separately.
Your ledger stays plain text files on your machine. Fava only reads and edits them.
Very little: keep Fava and Beancount updated and your files backed up. Reports and charts regenerate from the files every time.
A server you run - Docker, binaries or a NixOS module - hosting Git repositories with issues, pull requests and a web interface.
Repositories, issues and user accounts live on your server. Nothing depends on a hosted forge.
Updates, storage, backups and user administration. The project describes itself as community-governed; from v9.0 it is GPL v3-or-later.

tools/freshrss.heading: Your feeds, one reader you host.

qas.a: A small PHP web app - Docker or a classic web-server install - plus any compatible reader app on your devices.
Your subscriptions and read state live in your own database. Per its README it supports WebSub push from compatible sources.
Updates and a database backup. Pair it with a mobile reader app for reading away from the browser.

tools/gotify.heading: Push notifications without a commercial middleman.

qas.a: A small server (Docker or a binary) with a web interface and an Android app. Other services send messages through its HTTP API.
Messages pass through your server only - no commercial push service sees their contents. Each application gets its own revocable token.
The server, its tokens and updates. Keep it reachable from the services that alert you; it is simple by design.

tools/grafana.heading: Dashboards on top of the data you already have.

qas.a: A server - Docker, packages or a NixOS module - that reads from sources such as Prometheus, Loki and InfluxDB rather than storing everything itself.
Dashboard definitions and alerts live on your Grafana server; the underlying metrics stay in whichever database you connect.
The Grafana server, its data-source connections and dashboard upkeep. Dashboards survive swapping the database behind them. Grafana Labs sells cloud and enterprise offerings separately.
A dedicated device (a Raspberry Pi or similar), a container, or a VM. It connects compatible devices and services into dashboards and automations.
Configuration, history and automations live on your device. It favors local control, but some integrations still depend on vendor clouds - check each device rather than assuming offline operation.
Updates, occasional breaking-change notes, and the devices themselves. Start with a few integrations and grow deliberately.

tools/homepage.heading: A front door for your server.

qas.a: A Docker container or a Node.js service next to the things it links to. Everything is configured in a few readable YAML files.
Only configuration lives in Homepage; it pulls live status and widgets from over a hundred self-hosted apps without holding their data.
A YAML file and container updates. Widgets need API tokens for the apps they show - treat those tokens as secrets.

tools/immich.heading: A self-hosted alternative to Google Photos.

qas.a: A Docker Compose stack on a server with real storage, plus the mobile apps that upload straight from your phone.
Originals, albums, facial-recognition data and search indexes live on your server. Automatic backup runs from your phone to your machine, not a vendor cloud.
A multi-container stack: updates, storage growth and tested backups of both the files and the database. Budget real time for it.
A server you run - packages, Docker or the official install script - plus apps on phones, TVs and browsers.
Your library and watch state live on your server. It is a fully community-run fork of Emby with no premium tier and no tracking.
Server updates, library organization and transcoding horsepower if your clients need it. Everything is free; support goes to the project.
A Docker Compose stack: the app, a Meilisearch index for full-text search, and optional AI tagging.
Saved links, notes, images and PDFs are crawled and stored on your server - search still works when the original page disappears.
The Compose stack, storage for archived pages, and updates. Automatic AI tagging is optional and needs a model provider you choose.

tools/kitchenowl.heading: Shopping lists and recipes for a household.

qas.a: A server you host with web and mobile clients against it. Built for a household, not a team wiki.
Lists, recipes and meal plans live on your server.
Updates and a backup. Note that upstream still labels the project public alpha, not production-ready - expect rough edges.
A small web app you host - Docker is the common route.
Service visits, repairs, fuel fill-ups and odometer history stay on your own machine.
Very little: updates and a backup of its data. Try the project's demo first if you are unsure the workflow fits.
A server you run - Docker is standard - with web access for the household.
Recipes, tags, cookbooks, meal plans and shopping lists live on your server. Importing from a URL parses the page into ingredients, steps and a photo.
Updates and a database backup. AGPLv3-licensed.

tools/netbird.heading: A private network over WireGuard, no open ports.

qas.a: A management server you host (or the project's hosted service) plus a small client on each machine. Peers reach each other directly by name, wherever they are.
Peer registry, groups, access rules and DNS live on your management server; traffic flows directly between your machines over WireGuard.
The management stack and client updates. The admin dashboard handles peers, groups, access rules and routes - plan those before inviting a fleet.

tools/nextcloud.heading: A collaboration hub on your own server.

qas.a: A full server stack - the All-in-One Docker image is the documented easy route, classic installs and a NixOS module exist too.
Files, calendars, contacts and mail live on your server and sync to desktop and mobile clients. Link sharing, co-editing and calls stay inside your account.
A full stack rather than one container: updates across it, storage, backups and app compatibility at upgrade time. Nextcloud GmbH sells enterprise support separately.
Your own machine - Linux, macOS or Windows - with enough memory for the models you pick. GPU use is handled for you when available.
Models and chats stay on your machine. A local API on port 11434 serves them to other apps; many local-AI frontends expect exactly this backend.
Model storage grows fast - watch disk space. Updates are a single binary or service restart. MIT-licensed.

tools/omni-tools.heading: Everyday file jobs without online converters.

qas.a: A Docker container or a build from source, serving one browser interface for PDF operations, image conversion and text jobs.
The project says file processing happens on the client - your files are not sent to a server for the work itself.
A container and its updates. A good first self-host: low risk, immediate use.
A Docker Compose stack: the app, a database and a document queue. Drop files into its consumption folder and it OCRs, tags and files them.
Scans, OCR text, tags and the full-text index live on your server.
The stack, storage growth and backups of both documents and database. Worth the setup if paper keeps piling up.

tools/penpot.heading: Design and prototype in the browser, self-hostable.

qas.a: Your browser against the project's hosted service, or a Docker stack you run yourself. MPL-2.0 licensed.
On penpot.app, files live on the project's hosted service (run by the project, separate from this listing's focus). Self-hosted, they live on your server.
Self-hosting means the Docker stack, updates and backups. Designers and developers work in the same files either way.
A database server - packages, Docker or a NixOS module. This listing covers the 8.4 series, not the cluster, monitoring or paid-support products.
Your databases live on your server. GPLv2 with included components under their own notices.
A production database: updates, backups, replication if you need it. Check the documented telemetry settings during setup.

tools/pi-hole.heading: Network-wide DNS filtering from one small box.

qas.a: A Raspberry Pi, a small Linux server or a Docker container that your devices use for DNS - including devices that cannot run browser extensions.
Blocklists, rules and query logs live on your Pi-hole. Nothing routes through an outside filter service.
Updates, blocklist choices and router DNS settings. It is not a firewall or VPN: DNS filtering cannot remove every ad inside an allowed site or app.

tools/plausible.heading: Analytics without cookies or consent banners.

qas.a: The Community Edition you self-host (Docker), or the project's paid hosted service. Sites add a small script.
Traffic data lives in your own database; it collects no personal data, so sites can skip the consent banner.
The Community Edition stack and its updates. Self-hosting is free; the hosted version is a separate paid offering.

tools/postgresql.heading: A relational database with a decades-long track record.

qas.a: A server, a container or your development machine - packages for every platform, plus the psql terminal client.
Your databases live on your server. The core uses the permissive PostgreSQL License; extensions carry their own licenses.
A serious database if it holds real data: updates, backups and storage. For a graphical client, pair it with a tool such as DBeaver.
A Python server you run - packages, Docker or source - that manages authentication tokens and policies for applications and networks.
Tokens, policies and user assignments live in your own database. It works with existing user directories rather than replacing them.
An authentication service people depend on: updates, backups and recovery planning. AGPLv3; NetKnights sells enterprise packages and support separately.

tools/radicale.heading: CalDAV and CardDAV without the groupware.

qas.a: A small Python server you run. Keep using your compatible calendar and address-book apps on your devices - its web interface only manages collections.
Calendars and contacts live on your server and sync to your clients over CalDAV and CardDAV.
Very little: updates and a backup of its storage folder. Deliberately focused - not a mail or full groupware suite.

tools/scrutiny.heading: See a dying disk before it takes data with it.

qas.a: A web dashboard (Docker or binary) plus small collector agents on machines with drives you care about. It wraps smartd/smartctl data.
S.M.A.R.T. history, temperatures and wear data live on your Scrutiny server.
The dashboard, the collectors and alert settings. MIT-licensed; pairs naturally with a notification service such as Gotify.

tools/silverbullet.heading: A knowledge base that stays plain Markdown.

qas.a: A server you run - Docker, Deno or a NixOS module - used through the browser. Notes are Markdown files with links and queries.
The underlying files remain yours to edit, back up or move elsewhere; the extension and scripting system builds on top of them.
Updates and your own file backups. It rewards people who like shaping their own workflows.

tools/syncthing.heading: Folders in sync, no third-party cloud.

qas.a: Runs on each device you want to sync - laptop, phone, server. Devices pair by exchanging keys; traffic is encrypted end to end.
Your files exist only on your devices - nothing is stored on a third party's servers. File versioning options protect against accidental deletes and overwrites.
Client updates on each device and occasional conflict resolution. No central server to maintain unless you add one as another peer.

tools/technitium.heading: A full DNS server with a web console.

qas.a: A .NET application on a Linux or Windows machine, managed through its web console. Handles recursive and authoritative DNS.
Zones, blocklists and query logs live on your server. It speaks DNS-over-HTTPS, DNS-over-TLS and DNS-over-QUIC.
Updates, blocklist choices and router DNS settings. GPLv3; can run primary and secondary zones with clustering if you outgrow one box.

tools/trilium-notes.heading: A large knowledge base, structured as a tree.

qas.a: A desktop app, a self-hosted server for sync and web access, or both - desktop apps can sync with your server.
Notes, links, attributes and revisions live in your own database. A note can appear in more than one place without duplication.
Updates and database backups. This is a structured, power-user tool - richer than plain-Markdown notes.
A Node.js app with a PostgreSQL database, self-hosted - Docker is the documented route.
Traffic, referrers and events live in your own database, with no cookies and no personal data collection.
The app, its database and updates. Focused on simplicity: one clean dashboard rather than a maze of reports.

tools/uptime-kuma.heading: Know when things go down, before others tell you.

qas.a: A Docker container or Node.js app that checks websites, ports and services on a schedule.
Monitor definitions, response-time history and status pages live on your server. Status pages give others a place to check without dashboard access.
The container, its alert channels (services such as Gotify) and updates. An availability monitor, not a replacement for full metrics.

tools/vaultwarden.heading: Bitwarden apps, a server you can carry.

qas.a: A single Rust server - far lighter than the official Bitwarden server - that runs comfortably on a small VPS or home server, with the official Bitwarden apps and extensions as clients.
Your vault lives on your server, encrypted the same way the official clients expect. This is a community implementation of the API, not a Bitwarden product.
Your vault is the crown jewels: HTTPS is effectively required, updates matter, and backups of the database and attachments are non-negotiable.

tools/victoriametrics.heading: Fast time-series storage that pairs with Grafana.

qas.a: A single-node server (binary, Docker or packages). This page covers the open-source single-node server, not the enterprise features or VictoriaMetrics Cloud.
Metrics live on your server; query it with its API or point Grafana at it for dashboards.
The server, storage growth and retention settings. Apache-2.0 community code; enterprise and cloud are separate offerings.

tools/vikunja.heading: Tasks and projects, list or board.

qas.a: A server you self-host (Docker documented) or the project's hosted service, used through its web app.
Tasks, due dates, labels and assignments live on your server. Several views let the same plan work as a task list or a project board.
The server stack, updates and a database backup. Core server and web app are AGPL-3.0-or-later.

tools/warpgate.heading: One door for SSH, databases and web admin.

qas.a: A bastion host you run: point SSH, HTTPS, MySQL and PostgreSQL clients at Warpgate instead of handing every admin credentials for every server.
User roles, target definitions and session recordings live on your Warpgate host - which makes it a high-value system to protect.
A security-critical service: updates, hardening and careful role management. Session recording and access rules are the payoff.
